## **1. Introduction & Executive Summary** ### **1.1 Introduction** From the end of last year when gold seemed to be threatening the $1,500 barrier, a major recovery took place, with the price in late February breaching the $1,780 mark. This broadly mirrored a turnaround in investment, as ETFs holdings rose to a record high and as the net ‘investor’ long on Comex grew strongly. To an extent, this recovery was based on the cessation of earlier drivers, which included ‘forced’ selling resulting from funds facing redemptions or an urgent need to raise cash. However, new developments were arguably of more importance. One was the European Central Bank’s liquidity injection in late December and its late February long term refinancing operation. Perhaps of even greater significance was the announcement on 25th January by the US Federal Reserve that it was unlikely to raise interest rates until at least late 2014, more than a year beyond its previous guidance. Since February however, a marked retracement of well over $100 has occurred. Much of the initial drop was driven by statements by Fed chairman Bernanke on 29th February which were seen as ruling out imminent quantitative easing. The severity of this early March drop was in part just the product of profit taking and stop loss selling. However, the market’s sensitivity to US monetary policy was again illustrated when comments from the FOMC on 13th March that acknowledged economic optimism, again lessening the possibility of further QE, led to a further bout of price weakness. On top of the direct impact of both announcements on investment, interlinked dollar strength also boosted investor selling. We would not be surprised if such volatility were to continue, in part as investors’ interpretation of the impact of macro economic news on gold seems to be increasingly variable. Despite this noise, clear longer term trends remain discernible and, on balance, we believe there is a strong chance that the long term bull market has yet to run out of steam. However, recent months have highlighted sensitivity to the macro economic backdrop and fully justify our scenario-based approach; developments in November/December mirrored longer run possibilities under our bearish Scenario C, whilst events in January/February took us for a while more into the bullish environment of Scenario B. Whether either of these two or our core Base Case Scenario proves to be the actual outcome will therefore have profound implications for gold. |

Much of the agent of change would be investment, although in 2012 this could actually see a rise under this scenario.  However, that is only down to gains for implied net investment, which in turn reflects no immediate repetition of the heavy redemptions seen in late 2011; all other areas of investment are forecast to register losses.  The slide in World Investment becomes more pronounced in 2013 and 2014, chiefly as physical investment falls heavily.  The main causes of this slide include the absence of inflationary pressures and a rise in the US dollar.  Nonetheless, even by 2014, World Investment remains well over the 1,000 tonne mark thanks to such factors as persistent bargain hunting and concerns over the solidity of conventional assets. 

We have raised prices for each forecast year since the last report and this largely reflects the higher starting point this year that arose from the surprisingly resilient conditions seen in the opening month or so. 

### **1.2 The Base Case Scenario** 

In the wake of last year’s record of 2,811 tonnes, **mine production** looks set to post successive all time highs in each forecast year, with volumes in 2014 almost reaching 3,100 tonnes and with much of these gains originating in the Americas.  The high price environment has allowed for the redevelopment of historic mines and has given a strong stimulus to small-scale and informal mining.  However, of more importance for these increases is a strong project pipeline; it is this that enables growth in total output to occur in the final year, despite the then projected sharp retreat in the gold price.  Since the last report in November, estimates for each year have been shaded back by around 25 tonnes in response to minor delays in development and construction at several projects. 

Even though investor and management aversion to **producer hedging** remains intact, we believe this could grow and, by 2014, on a net basis exceed 120 tonnes.  Much of the initial growth will stem from counterparty banks’ delta hedge on opti

ons increasing, ongoing project hedging and limited de-hedging from legacy positions.  As we expect to see prices start falling later on, producers should begin to cautiously hedge to protect revenues and for this momentum to build.  Estimates for net hedging in each year have been cut slightly since the last report, chiefly as the price peak and then retreat have been postponed. 

Following modest losses in the last two years, **scrap supply** this year is forecast to see growth of around 10% and then a rise almost as strong in 2013, taking 









that year to a record 1,935 tonnes.  Recent sluggish levels were in part caused by some sellers holding back in anticipation of higher future prices and it is the release of this material plus the extra supply generated by the rise in the gold price, higher distress selling and improved collection facilities that drive levels to all time highs.  The forecast drop in the price in 2014 and the growing issue of near-market stock depletion then gives a 20% decline in scrap that year.  Since the last report, scrap has been trimmed in 2012 and notably raised in 2013 and 2014 due mainly to our revised price outlook. 

It is of note that the projected 2013 figure for scrap will exceed that year’s estimate for **jewellery fabrication** as higher prices and sluggish economic growth in several countries generate losses this year and next of around 5% for this area of offtake.  Losses are widespread, with the only main exception being China, where investment-related demand should enable growth to occur in both years.  Looking ahead to 2014 however and we expect a recovery to occur as the marked slide in the price, accompanied by improving economic growth, enable growth in offtake to over 2,100 tonnes.  Whilst this may be a six-year high, levels could be restrained by patchy investment-related buying against a backdrop of sliding prices and by uncertainty over western-style jewellery’s reaction to a lower price environment.  The main revisions since the last report are hefty cuts for offtake in 2013 and 2014 due to those years’ now far higher price projections. 

**Other fabrication** is forecast to rise this year, hold steady in 2013 but then fall notably in 2014, chiefly due to our expected path for coin demand.  In contrast, industrial fabrication should see slight growth in each forecast year as gains for electronics just outweigh structural losses in dentistry and a patchy performance from other industrial & decorative demand. 

Net **official sector purchases** are forecast to remain at an elevated level this year but then slide notably in both 2013 and 2014, with the latter year finishing below 200 tonnes.  Much of the buying will come from ongoing interest from central banks outside the Central Bank Gold Agreement, stemming from a desire to diversify away from fiat currencies and for some specifically away from the US dollar.  Their gross buying should in fact be more buoyant than the headline numbers mi

ght suggest as we expect banks within the CBGA to resume selling later on once the Eurozone crisis has passed, interest rates are rising and through many still being “overweight” in gold. ### **1.4 Scenario C** Scenario C is our most bearish take on possible outcomes. It chiefly differs by dint of inflation failing to become a

problem and the world economy staying weak (but not so ill as to raise new, stark fears on sovereign debt or bank failures).  Such conditions could raise the relative appeal of US treasuries, in turn boosting the dollar and triggering a slide in gold prices to an annual average of just $1,040 in 2014.  The chief agent within the gold market of that fall would be the slump in World Investment, which we see dropping from 1,751 tonnes in 2012 to 1,137 tonnes in 2014, with the collapse in western bar demand a key feature. The global total, however, would only hit a six-year low, thereby staying well above historic norms thanks to notable ‘bargain hunting’ in many markets. 

With the price in full retreat however and despite the worst economic outlook, jewellery demand recovers strongly with the 2014 estimate a nine-year high. Inversely, scrap falls steadily to a seven-year low by 2014.  Mine output, however, tracks broadly sideways as the benefits of the project pipeline are countered by the closure of some more mature operations.  It is also of note that the lower price environment would mean producer hedging could prove substantial. 

In line with the increase to our price forecasts in each year since the last report, jewellery demand has been cut slightly and scrap raised for all years.  Projections for World Investment have also been substantially increased, particularly in 2014.  In contrast, mine production and producing hedging have been trimmed.

## **2.  Price Forecast & Economic Assumptions** 

### **2.1 Introduction** 

Thomson Reuters GFMS’ views for the forecast period are presented in the form of three probability-weighted scenarios, namely the Base Case Scenario, Scenario B and Scenario C.  Under our **Base Case** , we expect a slowdown in world GDP growth this year.  This will mainly be driven by the ongoing sovereign debt crisis in Europe, fiscal policy tightening in places and a reduction in industrial production in major advanced economies.  Although developing countries continue to expand, their growth is likely to moderate due to tight monetary conditions in a number of places and downward pressure on external demand stemming from economic and financial problems in industrialised countries.  Nevertheless, we expect the world economy to improve gradually over the final two years of our forecast.  We view this as the most likely scenario, with a 45% probability.
